entry.title: The 13 rules from Reality Transurfing that rewired my whole life
entry.content:
Effort was never the variable, and you have known this for years.

You have watched people out-work you and finish exactly where they started, and you have watched people who visibly try less walk away with the whole board. Luck, timing, connections: those are the three explanations available to someone who does not want to look any further, and you have used all of them.

I am not standing above you on this. I spent eleven years with the effort dial turned as far as it goes, making better work every single year in a direction I had never once chosen on purpose. I was out-working people and finishing exactly where I started, except I had nicer photos to show for it.

The book that moved me is called Reality Transurfing. A Russian named Vadim Zeland wrote it, and it holds the most precise description of self-sabotage I have found anywhere. It explains, mechanically, why the thing you want most is the thing that keeps sliding away from you, and it does that without a single line of the motivational scaffolding the cover leads you to expect.

I have read it multiple times.

So here are the thirteen ideas in it.

This will take a while. It is not the kind of thing you skim in a queue and forget by lunch. Bookmark it, read it with something to write on, and come back to it every now and then.

Let's begin.

I. Your mind is a transmitter and reality tunes to the signal

The eradiation of mental energy induces the materialization of the variation.

Zeland's model holds that every possible version of your life already exists, sitting there like branches on a tree, and you do not construct the branch you end up on. You tune to it.

The transmitter is your own running commentary, the one nobody supervises. Whatever it broadcasts all day is what selects the branch.

You can leave the metaphysics alone and still run the experiment. Spend one day writing down what your internal monologue says about your work, your money, and your body. Most people find the results genuinely unpleasant, because they have been transmitting the same three complaints for a decade while calling it realism.

His conclusion: You cannot rewrite the branch you are standing on. You change what you transmit, and you step onto a different one.

II. Some things feed on your attention and cannot tell love from hate

When enough people think about the same thing, Zeland says that thing becomes a structure with an appetite. He calls them pendulums. They have no consciousness and exactly one purpose, which is to draw energy out of whoever feeds them.

In order to get rid of a pendulum, first, you need to admit that it exists and it has a right to do so. You have to calm down and lose interest towards it i.e. ignore it. By doing so you will deprive it of your mental energy.

The structure has no preference between your love and your hate. Fighting one feeds it precisely as well as joining it does. Both taste the same going down.

The competitor you check every morning before your own numbers is a pendulum. The argument you have sworn off twice and replied to four times is a pendulum. The niche you post in, chosen by whoever happened to be winning the month you started, is a pendulum wearing your career like a coat.

Strip the branding and it is all the same dopamine loop with a different skin.

You cannot beat one, and you cannot outrun one. You can only bore it, and boredom is the hardest thing on earth to fake, because the structure is built to read your pulse.

III. Momentum is fragile and most people kill it in the first four seconds

By accepting and transmitting the negative energy you create your individual hell. By accepting and transmitting the positive energy you create your individual heaven.

The third rule concerns what Zeland calls the Wave of Luck, and the unglamorous claim underneath it is that a run of good outcomes only builds from a first success you actually let yourself register.

Ambitious people are constitutionally incapable of this. The win lands, they give it four seconds, and they are back inside whatever is broken.

His instruction here is almost embarrassingly domestic. Close your mind to bad news and open it to good. Nurse the small changes. Those are the early signal of the wave, and treating them with contempt is how you kill it before it forms.

IV. Wanting it too much is the mechanism that removes it

In order to get in balance with the outside world, have freedom from pendulums and freely fulfill your desires — one needs to reduce the importance.

This is the engine of the whole book and the rule everyone who reads it quotes back to me.

Care about something too much and you create what Zeland calls excess potential, a pressure difference between that thing and everything around it. Equilibrium forces then move to level the pressure, and they level it against you, because you are the one holding the imbalance. The correction always arrives in the shape opposite to the intent that produced it.

You have watched this run in both directions without having a name for it. The round you desperately needed never closed. The client you were relaxed about signed on the first call. The message you rewrote nine times arrived reading exactly like a message somebody rewrote nine times.

The grip is the problem. Not the goal.

Effort tightens the grip, which is why turning it up has never once fixed this for you.

V. React to the disaster and you get written into it

Do not let any negative information into your layer of the world, intentionally ignore it, deprive it of attention and don't engage with interest.

Zeland calls this induced transition. Respond emotionally to a bad event and you move onto the line of life where that class of event is ordinary. You begin as a spectator to somebody else's catastrophe and end up cast in your own.

The layer of the world you live in is assembled from what you let in, which is a smaller and stranger quantity than what exists.

He is careful to separate this from avoidance. You do not fight the thing and you do not flee it. You go empty in its direction, and it stops finding you interesting.

VI. The body files its report before the mind builds its case

It is necessary to listen to the state of spiritual discomfort. If you have to persuade yourself, then the Soul says "no".

Here is where the chapter title comes from, and it contains the single most useful sentence in the book.

Zeland's claim is that some part of you can see branches you have not stepped onto yet, and it reports back in a register the mind barely registers. A vague comfort, or a vague weight. It arrives as a temperature rather than an argument.

The mind is loud and the weight is quiet, which is why almost nobody catches it. The test, though, is clean, and it is falsifiable inside sixty seconds.

If you had to talk yourself into it, that is your answer.

Run it against the last three large decisions you made. You already know which one it flags.

VII. Everything should be done in the easiest way available to you

In accordance with the principle of moving with the current, everything should be done in the easiest and simplest way.

Zeland lays out the two failure modes plainly. Drift like a paper boat and beg the world for outcomes, or row against the current and convert your life into a permanent war with everything in it.

His third option reads as heresy to anyone who built an identity on effort. Do not ask, do not demand, do not fight. Decide, then move, and take the path of least resistance the entire way.

The correct solution is almost always the simple one sitting on the surface. A mind under stress will reliably reach past it for something more complicated, because complicated feels like it deserves the reward more.

He attaches one instruction for the road. Watch for signs. A line of life gives you the feeling that something is off before it turns, and that feeling arrives well before the evidence does.

VIII. Deciding and wanting are different organs

Our wishes are realized by the External Intention, i.e. intention to own, our deep belief and concentration on how the goal is realized by itself.

Zeland splits intention in two, and the distinction explains why most goal-setting dies on contact.

Internal intention is the determination to act. That is you, pushing the world.

External intention is the determination to own, which is a settled certainty about how circumstances arrange themselves around something already yours.

He defines it as clarity without words, knowledge without faith, confidence without hesitation. It never arrives as an act of will. It shows up on the day the soul and the mind stop arguing about whether you are permitted to have the thing.

Which means the work is not more force. It is clearing out the excess potential and the pendulums that keep the argument running.

IX. You are running a slideshow and you did not choose the slides

Create yourself a positive slide pleasant to your soul and mind. Do not look at the slide as a picture, but live in it, at least virtually.

A slide is a distorted picture of reality you carry around with you. Zeland's point is that you already have dozens and consented to none of them.

Negative slides form when you care too much what other people see. They work as a magnifying glass held over your own worst features, and a slide carrying enough importance will drag you onto the branch where the picture is accurate.

The instruction is to build one deliberately and inhabit it rather than admire it. Add detail over time. Visit often.

One rule comes attached, and it is the one people break immediately. The slide has to be yours. A copy of someone else's dream will not hold, because no part of you wants it.

Which is most vision boards on this website, incidentally. Same wound, bigger mirror.

X. Visualise the stage, never the finish

Visualization in Transurfing is a vision of the process of realizing the current stage on the way to the goal.

Every manifestation book tells you to picture the outcome. Zeland says the opposite, and this is precisely where he separates from the crowd he keeps getting shelved next to.

You are not moved by the goal. You are moved by the visualisation of the process of moving toward it, at the stage you occupy right now.

So you break the path into stages and put your attention on the current one only. Picture it happening. Get interested in its mechanics. The end state is none of your business today.

He adds the part requiring patience. You will not be able to see how the goal gets done for a long time. Keep the slide running anyway. On the day it stops seeming impossible, meaning it has entered your comfort zone, the route appears.

XI. Charisma is the sound of a mind at peace with its own soul

Your Soul Fraile is the Holy Grail within you. In order to tune your mind to your Soul Fraile, you need to convince yourself that your soul is worthy of love in the first place.

Every soul has star sectors, the branches where you are entirely yourself. Reaching them requires you to stop running someone else's scenario, which is harder than it sounds, because the scenario is usually invisible from the inside.

The soul fraile is the specific set of attributes that make you you, buried under whatever the mind stacked on top. When the mind tunes to it, Zeland says you get a shine. That is his word, and it is his entire explanation for charisma. Harmony between soul and mind, visible from the outside, with no technique involved.

Pendulums work against this around the clock, because they need you measuring yourself against a standard. Discontent, envy, fear and resentment are their preferred food, and a person at home in themselves produces none of it.

XII. Your goal, your door, or somebody else's

Happiness comes during the journey to Your Goal through Your Door. Your Goal is something that gives you real pleasure, something that gives a feeling of joy, a feeling of a feast of life. Your Door is the path towards your goal on which you feel fascinated and inspired.

The last rule is worth the price of the book and almost nobody quotes it, because it is not fun.

Zeland's claim is that happiness exists on the line you are on now or it does not exist at all. The idea that you fight through obstacles to earn it later is a story pendulums tell, because a person postponing their life is a person permanently available for work.

Then the two tests, which are brutal in their simplicity.

If you want the goal in order to prove something, to yourself or to anyone else, it is not your goal.

If your mind has decided and your soul is uncomfortable, it is not your goal.

Somebody else's goal always feels like violence done to yourself, dressed as duty. It arrives wearing prestige, or fashion, or the appeal of being difficult to reach. Reaching it produces emptiness rather than joy, which is the cruel part, because by then you have spent the years.

I spent over a decade behind a camera. Campaigns for Samsung, Red Bull, Levis. I built an agency and hid behind the brand and the lenses and never once put my own face forward. The work speaks for itself, I said, which was true, and was the most convenient sentence available to me for about eleven years.

High standard. Real skill. Somebody else's door.

XIII. The world is a mirror and it answers slowly

The thoughts that we transmit inconspicuously transfer us (our material reality, our destiny) to the lines and sectors of the Space of Variations which literally correspond to our thoughts.

I use the mirror version of this, because a transmitter is an abstraction and a mirror is something you have stood in front of.

You hold the image. Reality holds the reflection. Everything that comes back to you is a report on what you have been showing it. What you asked for does not enter into it.

The reflection arrives late. Weeks, sometimes years. Most people change the image once, look up, find the old reflection still hanging there, and decide the whole idea is nonsense. Then they go back to broadcasting the same three complaints and the mirror goes back to confirming them.

It also has no taste. Your gripping goes in. So does your envy, and the part of you that has made peace with being overlooked. All of it comes back at the same flat resolution, and a man reading an accurate reflection will almost always call it bad luck.

Mine was accurate for a decade and I misread every frame of it. The phone rang. The invoices cleared. I read that as proof I was on the right line. What the mirror was actually reporting was a man who had arranged his whole working life so that nobody would ever have to ask him what he thought.

What changes

You will not become detached. Zeland is explicit that emotionlessness is not the goal, and a person performing serenity is only feeding a different pendulum.

What changes is resolution. You catch the grip while you are still gripping. The thing eating your mornings loses its hold the moment you can name it. And the question of whose goal you are carrying stops being philosophical, because the answer shows up in your chest before your mind has finished building its case.

Take one hour this week. Write down the five things you are chasing hardest, and beside each one write the name of the person who would be impressed. Where a name arrives faster than the goal does, you are looking at somebody else's door, and you have probably been paying rent on it for years.

Then change what you are holding up, and be patient with what comes back.

Rich

entry.title: The Degeneracy Economy
entry.content:
Yesterday, over a hundred people paid $199 to join a program that kicks them out if they don't launch a working product in 30 days. The money is gone the second you sign up. No refund policy.

You ship or you get thrown overboard and publicly shamed in front of the entire community.

The program is called Ship or Die. Two indie hackers, Marc Lou and Jack Friks , launched it less than 24 hours ago. As of right now, 134 people have paid. That's over $25,000 collected in a single day for an accountability product with zero curriculum and barely any content. Just a deadline and the threat of humiliation.

That should tell you everything about where we're headed.

A 22-year-old in Los Angeles bet his rent on whether Trump would tweet before 9am. He won. He paid rent. He did it again the next month. Polymarket did $9 billion in volume last year. Normal people with iPhones placing bets on elections, Fed rate decisions, whether a CEO gets fired.

Tuyo lets you buy now and pay maybe. You make payments when you feel like it, whenever you feel like it, with zero consequences if you don't. Just vibes and a prayer from the lender. How much financial nihilism do you want to put into consumer credit? Yes.

How did we get here

The boomers bought every house in the neighborhood, then voted to make sure nobody builds new ones. The average home costs 7x median income. Student debt crossed $1.7 trillion. Entry-level jobs require 3 years of experience while paying $42k in cities where a studio apartment costs $2,200 a month.

Gen Z did the math. The math ain't mathing.

When the traditional path to stability requires a decade of grinding just to reach the starting line your parents stood on at 23, gambling starts looking rational. The odds on the straight path are just as bad.

A 25-year-old saving $500 a month at 7% annual returns will have a house deposit in 14 years. She'll be 39. Her parents bought their first house at 26 with a single income and a handshake.

So she puts $200 on Polymarket instead. At least it's exciting. At least the outcome comes in 48 hours instead of 14 years. Sometimes when you FA it isn't till later the FO part of life hits you. But when the FO is already baked into the system, what's the difference.

Degeneracy as a business model

Every new fintech pitch deck has the same insight buried in slide 7: young people will accept worse terms if you make it feel like a game.

Gambling apps already figured this out. Sportsbooks spent $1.8 billion on advertising last year. DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM. They sell belonging. Watch the game with your boys. Put some skin in it. Make it mean something. The gambling part is just the delivery mechanism.

Now that playbook is bleeding into every vertical. Fitness. Civic engagement. Financial flexibility. Productivity. Every single one wraps a bet inside something that sounds responsible.

Strip the branding and it's all the same dopamine loop with a different skin.

The moral math

Boomers hoarded the assets. Pulled the ladder up. Now they call Gen Z lazy for not climbing something that was removed before they got to it.

Gen Z looked at the game, saw it was rigged, decided to play a different one. One where the house still wins but at least the results come fast and the interface has confetti animations.

The generation that inflated housing beyond reach and defunded every institution that used to create middle-class stability has no standing to lecture about financial responsibility. You folded an entire generation like cheap napkins and now you're surprised they came back feral.

Where this goes

We're early. Gambling will keep showing up in places you don't expect. Give it two years and someone will build a dating app where you stake money on getting a second date.

Every vertical that can add variable reward plus risk plus a leaderboard will. The engagement numbers are too good to pass up. The generation with all the screen time has been trained on dopamine loops since they were toddlers. Zero quit in their veins. Zero impulse control in their feed.

The degenerate economy is the logical conclusion of closing every normal door and leaving the casino open 24/7.

But the casino works both ways

The same loss aversion that makes people blow their paycheck on Polymarket is the same loss aversion that made 134 people pay $199 to ship a product.

The psychology is identical. The direction is different.

Steppa takes your gambling brain and points it at your health. You're not betting on sports. You're betting that you'll get off the couch. And 70% of the time, you win, because most people are too lazy to show up.

Ship or Die takes your gambling brain and points it at your output. You're not betting on an election. You're betting that you can build something real in 30 days. And you're doing it inside a community of 134 people who are all building at the same time. The deadline gets you moving. The people around you keep you honest. Miss it and you lose your money. Hit it and you walk out with something real that wouldn't have existed without the pressure.

The mechanism is cooked. But the result is you walking more, building more, shipping more. The degenerate economy is ugly. No question. But the people who understand the psychology and point it at themselves instead of a slot machine are going to come out of this decade in a very different position than the people who let it point at them.

I joined Ship or Die yesterday. I'm also starting a step challenge on Steppa this Monday.

Daily reminder you should bet on yourself.

entry.title: Your Brain Is Training Itself to Avoid Hard Things
entry.content:
You sat down to do the thing. Record the video. Write the sales page. Send the pitch. And immediately your body said no. Something in your chest tightened and you picked up your phone instead.

That feeling has a name. And a mechanism. And it gets worse every time you listen to it.

The avoidance loop

Tim Pychyl spent twenty years studying procrastination at Carleton University. His conclusion: procrastination is an emotion regulation problem. It has zero to do with time management or laziness.

When you think about doing something difficult, your brain generates a negative emotion. Self-doubt. Overwhelm. Fear that the result won't be good enough. Your amygdala flags the task as a threat. Same alarm system that would fire if someone broke into your house. Except the threat is a Google Doc.

So you escape. You clean something. Reorganize your Notion. Make a coffee. Open Instagram.

And the dread fades. You feel relief.

That relief is the trap. In psychology, behaviors that get rewarded get repeated. Your brain just learned that avoiding hard things produces a positive feeling. So next time you face something difficult, it defaults to the same move. Avoid. Relief. Repeat.

Every time you go through this cycle, you physically strengthen the neural pathway for avoidance. Like a trail in the woods that gets wider every time you walk it. Meanwhile the trail where you actually do the hard thing grows over.

Pychyl calls this the avoidance loop. Difficult task triggers negative emotion. You avoid the task. You feel relief. Next difficult task, same thing. The loop gets faster and more automatic each time.

The dopamine side

Andrew Huberman explained a related piece from the dopamine side. Your baseline level of dopamine determines your baseline motivation. When dopamine is low, everything feels like effort. When it sits at a healthy level, you can push through friction.

The problem: every time you escape into your phone or a distraction, you get a small dopamine hit from the easy thing. That momentarily spikes your dopamine, then drops it below where it was before. So you end up less motivated than when you started. The avoidance felt good for a minute, then made starting even harder.

This is why you can procrastinate for three hours and feel more exhausted than if you'd just done the work.

The two disguises

Your brain won't just let you sit on the couch. Sitting there doing nothing triggers guilt. Guilt is another negative emotion. Your amygdala wants to escape that too.

So it disguises the avoidance as productivity.

Perfectionism is the first disguise. Research shows that people who score higher on perfectionism are bigger procrastinators. The fear that the result won't meet the standard keeps you from starting at all. Pychyl's data showed that more perfectionist professors actually published fewer papers than their less perfectionist colleagues, even when controlling for work ethic. The standard became the excuse.

Productive procrastination is the second disguise. You spend the morning reorganizing your content calendar. You research microphones for two hours. You read a book about launching instead of writing the sales page. Your to-do list fills up with checkmarks. But the one thing that actually matters hasn't moved.

Pychyl calls this short-term mood repair. When a real task triggers anxiety, your brain swaps it for a safer task that still gives you a sense of accomplishment but carries zero risk of failure.

I wrote about how all of this shows up specifically in entrepreneurship here: If You Think Ayahuasca Brings Up Your Shadows, Try Entrepreneurship. Every shadow that surfaces when you try to build something with your name on it, fear of being seen, rejection, imposter syndrome, scarcity, all of them trigger this same avoidance loop. Entrepreneurship is a slow-drip version of facing your demons. On a random Tuesday afternoon when you're just trying to record a talking head reel.

What actually works

Pychyl's answer after twenty years of research is almost embarrassingly simple.

Just start. For ten minutes. Don't think about finishing. Don't think about the outcome. Just open the thing and work for ten minutes.

He ran a study where he gave 45 students pagers and paged them eight times a day for five days leading up to a deadline. Students consistently procrastinated on tasks they found difficult and replaced them with easier activities. They justified it all week. "I work better under pressure." "I'll feel more like it tomorrow."

When the deadline forced them to start, every single one said they wished they'd started earlier. The task was never as bad as they'd imagined.

Your brain's prediction about how bad something will feel is wrong almost every time. The dread of starting is almost always bigger than the thing itself.

Two specific moves that interrupt the loop:

First, name the emotion out loud. "I'm scared this won't be good enough." "I'm overwhelmed and don't know where to start." UCLA researchers found that labeling an emotion calms the amygdala. Shifts you from reacting to thinking. Simple, and it works fast.

Second, shrink the task until it's stupid. Don't tell yourself you need to write a 3,000 word article. Tell yourself to open the doc and write three sentences. Don't tell yourself you need to record a video. Tell yourself to set up the tripod and press record for ten minutes.

The compounding problem

Every time you go through the avoidance loop, the procrastination pathway in your brain gets stronger and the action pathway gets weaker. Like a muscle you stopped training.

But it compounds the other direction too. Every time you push through the first ten minutes, the avoidance circuit weakens and the action circuit strengthens. The friction gets smaller each time.

The founders who ship, who post, who launch, who put their face out there. They still feel the dread. They just got better at starting anyway.

Start before you feel ready. You'll never feel ready. Do it anyway.

entry.title: Distribution Ate Everything
entry.content:
OpenAI paid hundreds of millions of dollars for TBPN. A podcast. Two guys talking into microphones.

The most advanced AI lab on the planet paid more for a podcast than 99% of venture-backed startups will ever exit for.

a16z is building media arms. Paramount grabbed The Free Press for $150M. Stripe swallowed Indie Hackers. HubSpot bought The Hustle. Semafor raised $30M at a $330M valuation. Fox took Red Seat Ventures.

The smartest money on earth is making the same bet. And it's not on products.

It's on eyeballs.

A 14-year-old with Claude can ship an app in a weekend. Multiply that by a few million kids with laptops and wifi. They can build infinite apps, infinite content, infinite AI agents flooding every platform nonstop.

You can't print new eyeballs. There are 8 billion humans and 24 hours in a day. That's it. That's the global supply of attention. Production costs are collapsing to zero but CPMs keep climbing.

This is the distribution supercycle.

The old playbook is cooked

Meta CPMs crossed $40 in most B2C niches. Customer acquisition cost is up 222%. The average app converts at 1.2% on paid traffic. For every 1,000 people you pay to click, 988 ghost you.

Zuckerberg's new pitch is "give us your URL and we'll do the rest." When Meta's AI decides who sees your ads, creative quality and your willingness to stomach higher CPMs are all you have left. Their own data showed cost per conversion dropped 22.6% when they removed manual targeting. Good for their algorithm. Terrible for founders who relied on targeting precision to compete with bigger budgets.

When ads run through the same AI, the company that can pay the most per impression wins. Startups are not great at budget wars.

Billboards, TV, radio, print. Priced in 1998 dollars, performing to 1998 attention spans, still charging 2026 rates. The people still buying them confuse visibility with distribution.

Traditional influencers. $4,000 for a video averaging 3,000 views. Flat rate for a coin flip. Every one of these channels charges you the same whether the campaign prints money or dies in silence.

What actually works

Organic distribution. There are only four ways to play:

  1. Algorithmic text (X, Threads, LinkedIn, IG carousels)
  2. Algorithmic short-form video (Reels, TikTok, Shorts, Facebook Reels, LinkedIn video)
  3. Algorithmic long-form video (YouTube)
  4. Long-form video intentionally made to be clipped into short-form

That's it. If you don't have someone in your org who has genuinely figured out one of these four routes, you will get outrun by someone who has.

Kevin O'Leary used to pay customer acquisition managers $48,000. He now pays them $250,000. Because you can measure their output by revenue generated per week. Some of them go contractor and clear half a million a year. They know how to take content, cut it into a 59-second ad, and acquire 200 customers. Those people, usually in their early twenties, are the most valuable hires in business right now.

Clips are the new Facebook ads

Content distribution runs on clips now. Podcasts are clip factories. The average successful show produces 30 to 50 clips per episode and those clips reach 20x to 50x the audience of the full episode. Most fans consume the clips, not the show. The show is raw material. Clips are the distribution.

Both presidential campaigns in 2024 hired dedicated social clipping teams. The Harris campaign streamlined content approvals so clips of debate moments and rally reactions hit TikTok, Shorts, and Reels within minutes. 60-second clips reached more voters than any TV ad buy in history. Short-form distribution became an electoral strategy for the presidency of the United States.

The window

This is still early. UGC distribution and clip engines are where Facebook ads were in 2008. The founders who figure this out now will own their distribution for the next decade. The ones who keep renting attention from ad platforms will spend more every quarter for less.

The product is easy to copy. Distribution is the thing that compounds.
